rubrics.question_focus: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?

criteria.name: Atmosphere- and gravity-dependent flight feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons how a Cessna-like ordinary airplane would perform on different Solar System bodies based on atmospheric density, gravity, lift, stall speed, drag, and engine/propeller requirements.
criteria.1-2: Treats flight as mostly the same everywhere or gives arbitrary outcomes with little reference to atmosphere or gravity.
criteria.3-4: Mentions atmosphere or gravity but applies them inconsistently, e.g. claims normal flight on airless moons or ignores thin/dense atmospheres.
criteria.5-6: Correctly distinguishes broad cases such as airless bodies, Mars-like thin atmospheres, Titan/Venus-like dense atmospheres, and giant-planet atmospheres, but with limited quantitative or mechanistic support.
criteria.7-8: Explains lift, drag, stall speed, propeller/engine limits, and gravity well enough to justify most outcomes across major body types.
criteria.9-10: Provides physically coherent, body-specific reasoning tying density, gravity, temperature, pressure, composition, and aircraft performance to plausible flight or failure modes.

criteria.name: Coverage of major Solar System environments
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer covers the important categories and representative worlds relevant to flying an ordinary airplane over other Solar System bodies, rather than focusing narrowly on one or two examples.
criteria.1-2: Discusses only Earth or one other world, with no meaningful comparison across the Solar System.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few familiar bodies such as Mars, Venus, and Jupiter but omits major categories like airless moons, Titan, and ice giants.
criteria.5-6: Addresses most major categories: rocky planets, airless moons/asteroids, Titan, Venus, Mars, and gas/ice giants, but unevenly or with notable gaps.
criteria.7-8: Gives a clear comparative survey of the main Solar System body types and identifies representative outcomes for many specific worlds.
criteria.9-10: Systematically covers the dominant environments among large Solar System bodies, including Earth, Mars, Venus, Titan, airless moons, dwarf planets, and gas/ice giants, with distinct outcomes for each class.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response follows the downstream sequence from launch/release to attempted flight, loss of control, structural or environmental failure, crash, sinking, freezing, burning, or continued descent.
criteria.1-2: Gives isolated conclusions without causal sequence, such as simply saying the plane would crash or fly.
criteria.3-4: Includes some cause-and-effect but skips key stages or contradicts the likely timeline of events.
criteria.5-6: Provides plausible short causal chains for several worlds, though some transitions are vague or oversimplified.
criteria.7-8: Clearly traces multi-step outcomes for most environments, including initial lift, propulsion limits, control, environmental stress, and final fate.
criteria.9-10: Maintains detailed, internally consistent causal chains across diverse worlds, showing how immediate aerodynamics lead to longer-term consequences for the aircraft and pilot.

criteria.name: Environmental survivability and aircraft-system constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for non-aerodynamic constraints on an ordinary Cessna and pilot, including oxygen for combustion, temperature, pressure, corrosive atmospheres, radiation, winds, lack of runway, and absence of a solid surface.
criteria.1-2: Ignores survival and aircraft-system constraints, assuming the plane can operate normally if lift is possible.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few hazards, such as heat or lack of oxygen, but misses their implications for engine operation or pilot survival.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes several key constraints, including engine combustion, pressure, temperature, and atmosphere composition, but applies them unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Integrates aerodynamic and environmental limits, explaining why some places allow lift but still destroy, stall, suffocate, freeze, or crush the airplane/pilot.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly accounts for aircraft systems and human survivability alongside flight physics, distinguishing cases where the plane can glide, cannot power itself, is structurally destroyed, or is environmentally doomed.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain estimates while avoiding contradictions, impossible assumptions, or overconfident numerical claims about alien-world flight.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or confidently false claims, such as powered flight in vacuum or safe flight deep inside Jupiter.
criteria.3-4: Has several inconsistent statements or unsupported exact claims, though the overall idea may be partly recognizable.
criteria.5-6: Mostly avoids contradictions and uses cautious language, but still includes some overconfident or poorly reconciled assertions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes known physics from estimates, flags assumptions about launch altitude, aircraft configuration, and atmospheric level, and remains internally consistent.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, avoids spurious precision, states counterfactual assumptions explicitly, and keeps all conclusions consistent with the premise of an ordinary airplane in varied Solar System environments.

items.question: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?
human_answers: This is a common question. The Hubble operators get it a lot, and their FAQ page answers it (http://hubblesite.org/reference_desk/faq/answer.php.id=78&cat=topten).
items.original_question: 如果哈勃望远镜瞄准地球，图像会有多详细？

rubrics.question_focus: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Operational Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual of Hubble being aimed at Earth, including NASA/Hubble pointing rules, Earth-avoidance constraints, and why this is not a normal operating mode.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise as ordinary or ignores Hubble’s operational constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Hubble could point at Earth but gives vague or partially incorrect constraints.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that Earth-pointing is generally avoided due to brightness, safety, and mission design.
criteria.7-8: Explains Earth avoidance, instrument protection, target restrictions, and operational impracticality accurately.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual while distinguishing forbidden/risky operations from what might be physically possible in limited cases.

criteria.name: Optical and Detector Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the physical reasons Hubble would not produce useful Earth imagery, including focus, exposure, brightness, saturation, angular resolution, and instrument design for astronomical targets.
criteria.1-2: Gives fantasy claims such as Hubble taking perfect street-level images.
criteria.3-4: Notes images would be poor but gives little or wrong mechanism.
criteria.5-6: Mentions at least two relevant factors such as blur, saturation, or inappropriate exposure.
criteria.7-8: Connects detector saturation, exposure limits, focus/design assumptions, and resolution to degraded images.
criteria.9-10: Mechanistically explains how Hubble’s optics and instruments optimized for faint distant objects fail for bright, nearby, fast-changing Earth scenes.

criteria.name: Orbital Motion, Tracking, and Image Smear
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for Hubble’s low-Earth-orbit speed, rapid ground-track motion, tracking limitations, and resulting blur or smear during exposures.
criteria.1-2: Ignores orbital motion or assumes Hubble can hover over a target.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Hubble moves fast but does not connect it to imaging consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains that orbital speed would smear images during exposures.
criteria.7-8: Discusses fast relative motion, limited tracking/slew capability, and short viewing windows over any location.
criteria.9-10: Coherently traces orbit speed, exposure timing, pointing control, and target motion into severe practical limits on Earth imaging.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequences and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the counterfactual beyond the immediate act of pointing, covering likely data products, scientific value, hardware risk, policy implications, and comparison to Earth-observation satellites.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a one-sentence answer or makes unsupported dramatic claims.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but with weak causal links.
criteria.5-6: Covers likely poor images and limited usefulness compared with dedicated Earth satellites.
criteria.7-8: Explains downstream effects on data quality, scheduling, safety, and why Earth-observation satellites are better suited.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent chain from pointing decision to instrument response, operational disruption, data value, and institutional reasons it would not become a spy/Earth-monitoring platform.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming, distinguishes approximate from certain claims, and remains consistent with known facts about Hubble’s capabilities and FAQ-style explanations.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or confidently false claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes them with unsupported or conflicting statements.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with modest uncertainty but some imprecision.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates established facts from estimates and avoids common misconceptions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrated, internally consistent, and aligned with the known Hubble FAQ answer while adding plausible mechanism-level reasoning.

items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself.
items.original_question: 如果每艘船同时从地球水域移走，海平面会下降多少？

rubrics.question_focus: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?

criteria.name: Physical endpoint: global sea-level change
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly identifies the immediate global water-level effect of removing all ships from Earth's waters and estimates its magnitude using the relevant physics.
criteria.1-2: Claims a large sea-level change, tsunami, flooding, or no level change without applying displacement physics.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes ships displace water but gives a wildly incorrect magnitude or treats the effect as locally dramatic worldwide.
criteria.5-6: States that sea level would fall by a tiny amount, but lacks a defensible estimate or mixes correct reasoning with scale errors.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains that sea level drops by only a few microns because ships displace their own weight in water.
criteria.9-10: Gives a well-calibrated estimate near about six microns and clearly derives it from total ship mass, ocean area, and Archimedes' principle.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that every ship is removed from Earth's waters at once, without changing unrelated conditions or smuggling ships back in.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or substitutes a different scenario such as ships sinking, evaporating, or being destroyed in place.
criteria.3-4: Partially follows the premise but repeatedly conflates removal with sinking, grounding, or catastrophic ocean disturbance.
criteria.5-6: Mostly treats ships as removed, but leaves ambiguous where mass, cargo, crew, or displaced water go.
criteria.7-8: Consistently applies instantaneous removal and distinguishes it from sinking, unloading, or draining water.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the counterfactual boundary, noting what is and is not specified while avoiding unsupported extra assumptions.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage and causal depth
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer covers the key mechanisms caused by ship removal: displacement loss, local harbor effects, maritime transport interruption, ecological and pollution consequences, and economic/logistical cascades.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only one superficial consequence or focuses on irrelevant effects unrelated to ships in water.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few obvious effects but misses the central displacement mechanism or major downstream systems.
criteria.5-6: Includes displacement and some social or environmental effects, but with limited causal development.
criteria.7-8: Explains immediate physical effects plus plausible short- and medium-term impacts on ports, trade, fuel use, fishing, and pollution.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?

criteria.9-10: Precisely centers the analysis on conservation of energy and the ~1875 W heat input accumulating within the sealed system.

criteria.name: Thermal evolution and quantitative plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives a physically plausible account of temperature rise over time, including the role of air, box walls, heat capacity, and heat leakage to the environment.

criteria.9-10: Uses coherent energy/heat-capacity reasoning to distinguish ideal sealed-insulated behavior from realistic conductive heat loss and eventual equilibrium.

criteria.name: Sealed-box pressure, airflow, and internal environment mechanisms

criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates recirculation, temperature-driven pressure increase, possible moisture effects, and no significant oxygen consumption by the electric dryer.

criteria.name: Long-range failure modes and downstream effects

criteria.3-4: Lists possible hazards but with little causal ordering or realism.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some likely outcomes, such as overheating or shutdown, but does not connect them well.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control

criteria.1-2: Presents contradictory or overconfident claims incompatible with the setup.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of unknowns but still makes inconsistent or unjustified assertions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with limited caveats about materials or heat loss.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates assumptions and gives conditional outcomes without major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous consistency across the full causal chain and explicitly calibrates uncertainty around all major unspecified variables.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects.

criteria.9-10: Traces a coherent chain from disposal method to trap settling, pipe restriction, microbial breakdown, septic/municipal handling, and eventual maintenance outcomes.

criteria.name: Counterfactual fidelity and contradiction control

items.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway.
items.original_question: 如果你设法让立体声以两倍音速传播，当它飞过时，对于一个只是随意坐在某处的人来说，它听起来会是倒退的吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?

criteria.name: Endpoint Answer: Can It Be Heard?
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response gives the correct bottom-line answer for a stereo moving at twice the speed of sound: yes, technically it can be heard, but not as normal music arriving smoothly before it passes.
criteria.1-2: Gives the wrong endpoint, such as saying it would be completely silent or normally audible.
criteria.3-4: Says it might be heard but is vague or contradicts itself about when or how.
criteria.5-6: States that it could be heard, but gives only a partial explanation of the unusual conditions.
criteria.7-8: Correctly says yes, but mainly as a delayed, distorted, shock-associated sound rather than normal playback.
criteria.9-10: Clearly states the nuanced endpoint: yes, technically, but the listener would not hear ordinary music approaching; they would mostly hear a sudden Mach-cone/sonic-boom-like event and possibly distorted audio afterward.

criteria.name: Supersonic Sound Propagation Mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accurately explains how sound emitted by a source traveling at Mach 2 propagates relative to the moving stereo.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the speed-of-sound issue or treats sound as traveling instantaneously.
criteria.3-4: Mentions supersonic motion but incorrectly describes sound catching up ahead of the stereo.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that sound cannot travel ahead of the stereo, but lacks a clear wavefront explanation.
criteria.7-8: Explains that emitted sound waves trail behind and accumulate into a Mach cone.
criteria.9-10: Accurately describes the Mach 2 geometry: the stereo outruns its own sound, wavefronts form a trailing cone/shock structure, and a listener hears sound only when that cone reaches them.

criteria.name: Mach Cone, Sonic Boom, and Listener Timeline
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the causal sequence experienced by a stationary listener as the supersonic stereo passes.
criteria.1-2: Presents an impossible or reversed timeline, such as music being heard before any physical arrival cue.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a boom or delay but gives an unclear or inconsistent sequence.
criteria.5-6: Describes a delayed sound arrival but misses key features of the sudden shock front.
criteria.7-8: Gives a coherent timeline: silence before cone arrival, sudden boom or pressure jump, then possible trailing sound.
criteria.9-10: Provides a precise causal timeline: no advance warning by sound, the object may pass visually first, the Mach cone reaches the listener later depending on geometry, producing a sharp boom/compressed wavefront and only then any audible stereo content.

criteria.name: Audio Quality, Doppler Effects, and Distortion
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response addresses what the stereo’s music would sound like under the Mach 2 counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Assumes the music would sound normal and continuous.
criteria.3-4: Says it would be loud or distorted without explaining why.
criteria.5-6: Mentions Doppler shift or distortion but applies it incompletely or loosely.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the music would be highly compressed, shifted, overlapped, or disrupted by shock effects.
criteria.9-10: Accurately discusses that normal recognizable music is unlikely: wavefront pileup, nonlinear shock/boom dominance, extreme Doppler/time-compression effects, and source/air interaction would make the audio brief, distorted, and possibly overwhelmed.

criteria.name: Physical Plausibility and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response maintains internal consistency while acknowledging practical uncertainties about a stereo physically flying at Mach 2.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or ignores physical constraints entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mixes correct ideas with serious conflicts, such as both outrunning sound and hearing it normally ahead.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but omits practical caveats like shock damage, power, mounting, or air turbulence.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent counterfactual and notes realistic complications without derailing the answer.
criteria.9-10: Cleanly separates the counterfactual assumption from real-world feasibility, avoids contradictions, and calibrates uncertainty about survivability, loudness, shock strength, distance, atmosphere, and whether recognizable audio would remain.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it.
items.original_question: 以今天的技术，是否有可能发起无人回收航行者一号任务？

rubrics.question_focus: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?

criteria.name: Voyager 1 Baseline and Counterfactual Setup
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly grounds the scenario in Voyager 1's current status and defines what a one-way mission launched today would mean.
criteria.1-2: Misstates Voyager 1's location, direction, or status; treats the mission as routine or near-Earth.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Voyager 1 is far away but gives vague or inaccurate context about distance, speed, or trajectory.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object and outbound, but setup lacks quantitative or mission-specific framing.
criteria.7-8: Accurately frames Voyager 1 as extremely distant, outbound, and fast, making a modern chase mission exceptionally difficult.
criteria.9-10: Precisely grounds the counterfactual with distance, relative motion, one-way constraints, and the fact that no existing craft is on track to overtake it.

criteria.name: Propulsion, Delta-v, and Trajectory Feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the causal reasoning about whether a spacecraft launched today could catch Voyager 1, including propulsion limits, gravity assists, and travel times.
criteria.1-2: Ignores propulsion and trajectory mechanics or assumes catching Voyager 1 is easy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions speed or fuel limits but with major physical errors or no causal explanation.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that catching Voyager 1 requires extreme velocity, but only loosely discusses launch energy or assists.
criteria.7-8: Explains that a feasible intercept would need unusually high delta-v, careful gravity assists, or advanced propulsion, with long timescales.
criteria.9-10: Coherently analyzes relative velocity, launch energy, possible Oberth/gravity-assist strategies, and why current chemical missions would likely take decades or longer.

criteria.3-4: Lists a few mission challenges without showing how they evolve over time.

criteria.7-8: Connects long travel time to power decay, autonomy needs, communication constraints, tracking difficulty, and limited science return.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent end-to-end chain from launch through decades-long cruise to possible flyby/intercept, including power, thermal, autonomy, data return, and operational degradation.

criteria.name: Scientific and Practical Value Assessment
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly evaluates what such a one-way mission would achieve compared with alternatives.
criteria.1-2: Claims unrealistic benefits or ignores mission purpose entirely.
criteria.3-4: Gives generic statements about exploration with little relation to Voyager 1.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some possible value, such as inspecting Voyager 1 or studying interstellar space, but lacks tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Balances potential scientific/historical gains against enormous cost, risk, and limited return.
criteria.9-10: Clearly evaluates whether chasing Voyager 1 is justified, comparing possible inspection, interstellar-medium science, and symbolic value against cheaper or more productive mission designs.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming, handles unknowns appropriately, and remains internally consistent with known Voyager facts.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, impossible claims, or confident false conclusions.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but mixes it with unsupported or inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, though with vague numbers, minor contradictions, or overconfident feasibility judgments.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes known facts from estimates and avoids major contradictions about Voyager 1's speed, distance, and mission status.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainties in launch technology, travel time, and spacecraft survival while maintaining a consistent causal narrative throughout.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?

criteria.9-10: Gives a physically plausible chain from Earth-scale mass/radius and density to surface gravity, internal pressure, compaction/melting/fracture, and eventual planetary reconfiguration.

criteria.name: Long-range planetary consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects after the initial enlargement, including gravity at the surface, interaction with surroundings, atmosphere/volatiles if present, orbital implications, habitability, and what happens over geological timescales.
criteria.1-2: Only describes the visual appearance and gives no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few effects, such as 'it would be heavy' or 'people would die,' without causal development.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several consequences like gravity, impact on nearby objects, and habitability, but omits major long-term planetary processes.
criteria.7-8: Traces multiple downstream effects coherently, including surface gravity, atmospheric retention or absence, tides/orbits, and long-term reshaping.
criteria.9-10: Integrates immediate, intermediate, and long-term consequences into a coherent scenario, distinguishing dependence on placement, environment, composition, and timescale.

criteria.name: Quantitative plausibility and order-of-magnitude control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses reasonable estimates for size, density, mass, surface gravity, scaled feature sizes, and pressures without overclaiming precision.
criteria.1-2: Contains no quantitative reasoning or uses wildly impossible numbers that drive false conclusions.
criteria.3-4: Includes numbers but with major scale errors, such as confusing diameter with radius or ignoring density differences.
criteria.5-6: Uses some reasonable estimates, but calculations are sparse, approximate, or inconsistently applied.
criteria.7-8: Provides mostly sound order-of-magnitude estimates for mass, gravity, surface relief, and compression effects.
criteria.9-10: Uses concise, correct estimates to support the scenario, clearly marking assumptions such as bowling-ball density, Earth-sized radius, and whether holes are scaled.

criteria.name: Counterfactual consistency, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains the counterfactual premise consistently, separates assumptions from conclusions, avoids contradictions, and acknowledges uncertain branches such as exact bowling-ball composition or whether it replaces Earth versus appears elsewhere.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself or abandons the premise; presents impossible claims as certain without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Maintains the premise only loosely and gives overconfident or conflicting statements about composition, gravity, or survival.
criteria.5-6: Generally consistent but leaves key assumptions unstated or treats uncertain outcomes too definitively.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions and handles alternatives such as replacement of Earth, free space placement, or real-material collapse with few contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully preserves the counterfactual setup, flags uncertain material and environmental dependencies, and avoids unsupported certainty while still giving a decisive plausible account.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?

rubrics.question_focus: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?

criteria.name: Light-travel-time and observational geometry fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise of observers on the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, including distance, time delay, viewing geometry, and what epoch of Earth they would observe.
criteria.1-2: Ignores light-travel time or gives wildly incorrect distances/times; treats aliens as seeing Earth in real time.
criteria.3-4: Mentions delay or distance but with major errors or little impact on the scenario.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes a roughly 4-year delay from the nearest candidate system but applies it inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Accurately uses the Proxima/Alpha Centauri distance scale and explains that they see Earth and human activity several years in the past.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates distance, time delay, line of sight, and observational limits into all downstream claims.

criteria.name: Detectability of Earth, the Sun, and biosignatures
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of what aliens could plausibly infer about Earth using astronomy: the Sun, Earth as a planet, atmospheric composition, oceans, vegetation, and biosignatures.
criteria.1-2: Claims they would directly see cities, people, or continents with no telescope constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Earth or life signals but confuses brightness, resolution, or spectroscopy.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible observables such as the Sun, Earth’s orbit, or atmospheric gases, but with shallow mechanism.
criteria.7-8: Explains indirect detection through reflected light, transits or direct imaging, spectra, oxygen, water vapor, methane, and seasonal/color changes.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of detectability thresholds, angular separation, contrast with the Sun, instrumentation dependence, and biosignature ambiguity.

criteria.name: Technosignature and radio-signal reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly handles human technological detectability from a nearby exoplanet, including radio leakage, intentional transmissions, radar, city lights, and industrial atmospheric signals.
criteria.1-2: Assumes all human broadcasts, internet content, or visual details are easily observable.
criteria.3-4: Mentions radio or technology but greatly overstates detectability or ignores signal attenuation.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that some artificial signals may exist but gives limited detail on strength, directionality, or noise.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes weak broadcast leakage from stronger radar/intentional beams and notes city lights are extremely hard to resolve.
criteria.9-10: Accurately traces which technosignatures could reach them, their age window, inverse-square weakening, frequency issues, and dependence on alien receiver capability.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence under the alien-observer premise
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how coherently the answer links the counterfactual vantage point to downstream observations, inferences, and limitations without jumping to unsupported conclusions.
criteria.1-2: Provides disconnected facts or science-fiction claims with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose chain but repeatedly confuses observation, inference, and speculation.
criteria.5-6: Follows a mostly coherent sequence from distance to signals to possible conclusions, with gaps.
criteria.7-8: Clearly connects alien location, telescope capability, received photons/signals, data interpretation, and uncertainty.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a rigorous end-to-end causal model from emission/reflection on Earth to detection, analysis, and possible alien conclusions.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately qualifies unknowns, avoids overclaiming, and remains internally consistent about alien technology, nearby habitability, and observational feasibility.
criteria.1-2: States speculative claims as certain and contains direct contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Uses some caveats but mixes incompatible assumptions or unsupported certainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty about alien technology and habitability but inconsistently calibrates confidence.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates known astronomy from assumptions about alien instruments and civilization level.
criteria.9-10: Consistently quantifies or qualifies uncertainties, avoids contradictions, and presents multiple plausible observational regimes.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already.
items.original_question: 如果太阳突然熄灭，地球会发生什么？

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling for the Sun going dark
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer clearly defines and consistently reasons from the premise that the Sun suddenly stops emitting light/heat, while distinguishing this from the Sun physically disappearing or losing mass.
criteria.1-2: Confuses the premise, e.g. treats the Sun as exploding, vanishing, or Earth instantly freezing without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions the Sun going dark but mixes incompatible assumptions about light, heat, gravity, or mass.
criteria.5-6: Mostly assumes the Sun stops shining, but leaves key premise details ambiguous or occasionally inconsistent.
criteria.7-8: Clearly treats the Sun as no longer emitting radiation and mostly preserves gravity/orbits unless explicitly caveated.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames alternative interpretations, selects one, and keeps all downstream reasoning consistent with that premise.

criteria.name: Immediate physical consequences and timescales
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-term effects after the Sun goes out, including the roughly 8-minute light-travel delay, loss of daylight, temperature decline, and radiation changes.
criteria.1-2: Gives implausible instant effects with no timescale awareness.
criteria.3-4: Includes darkness or cold but misses the 8-minute delay and gives vague or incorrect timing.
criteria.5-6: Notes some correct immediate effects, but timing and mechanisms are incomplete or partially wrong.
criteria.7-8: Accurately covers the 8-minute delay, rapid darkness, and progressive cooling with reasonable timescales.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent sequence from first minutes to days/weeks, with accurate physical mechanisms and no exaggeration.

criteria.name: Earth climate, oceans, atmosphere, and habitability chain
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and plausibility of downstream Earth-system reasoning: surface cooling, weather collapse, freezing oceans, atmospheric changes, and possible refuges.
criteria.1-2: Claims all life or oceans vanish immediately, or gives fantasy outcomes unsupported by physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions freezing and death but lacks mechanisms, order, or realistic staging.
criteria.5-6: Covers major effects such as cooling, photosynthesis failure, and ocean freezing, but shallowly or with rough errors.
criteria.7-8: Explains staged collapse of climate, food webs, surface habitability, and oceans with plausible timing.
criteria.9-10: Integrates climate inertia, ocean heat capacity, geothermal heat, atmosphere behavior, and survival niches into a realistic long-range chain.

criteria.name: Biological and human civilization consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces effects on ecosystems, agriculture, energy systems, infrastructure, and potential human survival strategies under prolonged solar absence.
criteria.1-2: Only states that everyone dies or gives unsupported survival claims.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plant death or human hardship but omits food, energy, and ecological cascades.
criteria.5-6: Identifies photosynthesis collapse, food-chain failure, and human shelter needs, but with limited causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Connects ecosystem collapse to agriculture, power, heating, logistics, and underground/technological refuges.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced survival analysis including stored food, artificial light, nuclear/geothermal power, deep ocean vents, and long-term limits.

criteria.name: Long-range coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent causal timeline from minutes to years or longer, appropriately signals uncertainty, and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Is internally contradictory, temporally chaotic, or confidently asserts impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose sequence but frequent contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Presents a generally plausible timeline but with gaps, overconfident claims, or minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal progression and flags uncertain estimates or premise-dependent outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a robust long-range scenario with calibrated uncertainty, explicit assumptions, and no meaningful contradictions.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature.
items.original_question: 驾驶划艇穿过水银湖会是什么感觉？溴呢？液态镓？液态钨？液氮？液氦？

rubrics.question_focus: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?

criteria.name: Physical premise handling and phase-condition accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly establishes the counterfactual conditions required for lakes of mercury, bromine, gallium, tungsten, liquid nitrogen, and liquid helium, including temperature, pressure, phase stability, and what is or is not liquid under ordinary conditions.
criteria.1-2: Treats most substances as ordinary room-temperature lakes or gives major phase errors, such as liquid tungsten or helium at ambient conditions.
criteria.3-4: Identifies a few liquid-state requirements but misses several key conditions or mixes incompatible temperatures and pressures.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes the main liquid-state constraints for most substances, with some omissions or minor inaccuracies.
criteria.7-8: Accurately distinguishes room-temperature liquids from cryogenic or high-temperature cases and explains needed conditions for all six substances.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames each lake's required environment, including extreme heat for tungsten, near-room melting for gallium, cryogenic nitrogen/helium, and pressure-dependent helium behavior.

criteria.name: Rowing and boat-mechanics plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer reasons about buoyancy, density, viscosity, surface tension, wave behavior, drag, paddle effectiveness, and boat material survival in each liquid.
criteria.1-2: Gives fanciful or generic descriptions of rowing with little connection to fluid properties.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two relevant properties, such as density or viscosity, but applies them inconsistently across the liquids.
criteria.5-6: Provides plausible rowing implications for several lakes, including buoyancy and resistance, but lacks full comparative depth.
criteria.7-8: Connects each substance's density, viscosity, thermal state, and chemical behavior to realistic rowing difficulty and vessel design.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a coherent substance-by-substance mechanics analysis, including unusual effects such as high buoyancy in mercury, freezing/boiling hazards, dense molten metals, and cryogenic fluid behavior.

criteria.name: Human survivability and environmental hazard chains
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream hazards to a rower, including toxicity, corrosivity, vapor exposure, thermal injury, asphyxiation, fire or material failure, radiation-free assumptions, and protective requirements.
criteria.1-2: Ignores survivability or assumes a person can row normally despite lethal environments.
criteria.3-4: Mentions obvious danger but misses major hazard mechanisms for most liquids.
criteria.5-6: Covers several important hazards, such as bromine toxicity or cryogenic cold, but leaves gaps in causal consequences.
criteria.7-8: Explains the main lethal pathways for all or nearly all substances and ties them to necessary suits, atmosphere, and boat materials.
criteria.9-10: Provides a detailed, causally ordered hazard analysis for each lake, including fumes, burns, freezing, boiling, oxygen displacement, metal heat, and chemical attack.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence across the scenario
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer maintains internally consistent causal chains from the imposed lake conditions through fluid behavior, vessel interaction, local atmosphere, human constraints, and practical outcome.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, disconnected claims, or impossible sequences that undermine the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct facts but frequently breaks causal continuity or ignores consequences of stated conditions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly understandable chain of effects, though some implications are skipped or inconsistently followed.
criteria.7-8: Builds coherent cause-and-effect narratives for each liquid with few contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Sustains rigorous long-range reasoning throughout, ensuring every assumption about temperature, pressure, toxicity, and mechanics propagates consistently to the rowing experience.

criteria.name: Comparative coverage, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer covers all six substances proportionally, compares them meaningfully, avoids overclaiming, and flags uncertain or assumption-dependent points such as container pressure, atmosphere, boat materials, and scale.
criteria.1-2: Omits several substances, makes unsupported absolute claims, or contradicts known chemistry and physics.
criteria.3-4: Covers most substances superficially but has uneven detail, overconfidence, or unresolved inconsistencies.
criteria.5-6: Addresses all six with some comparison and caveats, though calibration and depth are uneven.
criteria.7-8: Compares all six clearly, distinguishes robust conclusions from assumption-dependent ones, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Balances concise coverage of every liquid with explicit caveats, calibrated uncertainty, and clean resolution of apparent conflicts such as gallium's near-room melting point or helium's special cryogenic requirements.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball.
items.original_question: 如果将 3,000 个弹力球从七层停车场扔到下面人行道上行走的人身上会怎样？如果这个人活下来，需要多少个弹力球才能杀死他？会发生什么伤害以及相关的犯罪是什么？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?

criteria.name: Fall physics and impact speed
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from a seven-story drop to the approximate speed and energy of individual Super Balls at impact.
criteria.1-2: Gives physically impossible or wildly exaggerated speeds, such as bullets, explosions, or lethal meteor-like impacts.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes the balls fall and gain speed but gives no credible estimate or badly misstates the scale.
criteria.5-6: Provides a roughly plausible fall speed or energy estimate but omits key assumptions such as height, air resistance, or ball mass.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates impact speed near 20 m/s and relates it to familiar thrown-ball speeds with minor omissions.
criteria.9-10: Accurately explains the seven-story fall, gravity, possible air resistance, and why each ball’s impact is comparable to a hard thrown bouncy ball.

criteria.name: Collective effect of 3,000 balls
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes between the modest impact of each ball and the cumulative effect of thousands arriving over an area and time interval.
criteria.1-2: Treats the 3,000 balls as a single crushing solid mass or ignores the number entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions many balls but gives an incoherent or unsupported conclusion about their combined effect.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that many small impacts are worse than one ball, but gives limited reasoning about distribution, timing, or hit probability.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the danger depends on how tightly they are dropped, how many hit the pedestrian, and whether impacts overlap.
criteria.9-10: Clearly models the swarm-like impact: individual low-mass strikes, possible dense clustering, multiple body hits, and cumulative nuisance or injury risk.

criteria.name: Human injury and likely outcome
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer gives a plausible assessment of harm to the pedestrian under realistic assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Claims certain death, total safety, or cartoonish outcomes without physical support.
criteria.3-4: States an outcome but with little connection to impact speed, ball mass, exposed body parts, or quantity.
criteria.5-6: Gives a broadly plausible result such as pain, bruising, or startle, but lacks nuance about sensitive areas.
criteria.7-8: Identifies likely pain, welts, bruises, eye/face risk, loss of balance, and low likelihood of fatal injury.
criteria.9-10: Balances severity carefully: most impacts are nonfatal but thousands could cause significant pain, minor injuries, eye damage, panic, or falls depending on concentration.

criteria.name: Secondary dynamics after impact
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for Super Balls’ elasticity, bouncing, scattering, and follow-on hazards after the initial impacts.
criteria.1-2: Ignores bouncing entirely or describes impossible behavior inconsistent with elastic balls.
criteria.3-4: Mentions bouncing but not how it affects the pedestrian or surroundings.
criteria.5-6: Notes that balls would rebound and scatter, creating some secondary nuisance or hazard.
criteria.7-8: Explains ricochets, repeated lower-energy impacts, rolling underfoot, and possible slipping or tripping.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the rebound phase coherently with the initial strike, including scattering, repeated collisions, footing hazards, and environmental dependence.

criteria.name: Assumptions, uncertainty, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer calibrates uncertainty and avoids contradictions while reasoning through the counterfactual scenario.
criteria.1-2: Contains major internal contradictions or presents unsupported certainty about unspecified details.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges few assumptions and mixes plausible claims with inconsistent ones.
criteria.5-6: States some relevant assumptions, such as height or ball size, but does not consistently use them.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags important variables including garage height, drop pattern, ball size, pedestrian posture, and protective clothing.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a coherent causal chain, quantifies where useful, distinguishes known from uncertain factors, and keeps conclusions consistent with the estimated physics.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and hydraulic setup
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the 10-meter drain at Challenger Deep and reasons from ocean pressure, head, aperture area, and flow limits rather than treating the ocean as instantly disappearing.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or assumes instantaneous/near-instant drainage without hydraulic reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes water drains through a 10-meter hole but gives only vague or physically dubious flow claims.
criteria.5-6: Uses pressure/head or hole area qualitatively and avoids instant-drain errors, but lacks reliable quantitative grounding.
criteria.7-8: Estimates flow using depth, pressure, and aperture area with mostly sound order-of-magnitude reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Accurately models the drain as a high-pressure, finite-area outflow, noting turbulence/discharge limits and changing head over time.

criteria.name: Timescale and sea-level trajectory
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly estimates how long ocean drainage would take and how sea level would decline over human, ecological, and geological timescales.
criteria.1-2: Gives wildly implausible timescales such as hours, days, or a few years with no correction.
criteria.3-4: States drainage is slow or long-term but provides no defensible scale or contradicts basic volume/flow constraints.
criteria.5-6: Provides a rough long timescale and recognizes declining head, but the magnitude or trajectory is only partly justified.
criteria.7-8: Gives a plausible order-of-magnitude timescale, e.g. hundreds of thousands to millions of years, with sea level falling slowly.
criteria.9-10: Connects ocean volume, flow rate, basin geometry, and decreasing pressure to a coherent multi-stage sea-level decline.

criteria.name: Immediate local effects at Challenger Deep
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-hole phenomena: extreme pressure, violent inflow, suction limited to the local region, structural crushing of objects near the drain, and effects on the trench environment.
criteria.1-2: Ignores local effects or describes impossible global whirlpools engulfing ships everywhere.
criteria.3-4: Mentions suction or whirlpools but exaggerates their global reach or misses pressure-driven crushing.
criteria.5-6: Identifies strong local currents and pressure near the hole but with limited mechanism detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains intense local inflow, turbulence, sediment disturbance, and damage to objects near the drain while limiting the effect spatially.
criteria.9-10: Precisely distinguishes local catastrophic flow near Challenger Deep from weak global currents and includes pressure/structural consequences.

criteria.name: Long-range Earth system consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces major downstream effects of slow ocean loss, including coastlines, climate, marine ecosystems, salinity, ocean circulation, exposed seafloor, hydrology, and geology.
criteria.1-2: Lists few consequences or relies on sensational unrelated disasters.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some effects such as dry seabeds or ecological collapse but without causal sequencing.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major downstream effects, though unevenly or with weak links between them.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent chain from falling sea level to habitat loss, climate shifts, altered circulation, exposed land bridges, and geological adjustment.
criteria.9-10: Integrates biological, climatic, hydrological, geomorphic, and human consequences across short, medium, and geological timescales.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles unknowns in the counterfactual, avoids internal contradictions, and clearly separates robust conclusions from speculative details.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible physics, or unsupported certainty throughout.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible claims but mixes them with contradictory or overconfident assertions.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent, with limited caveats, but leaves important assumptions implicit or inconsistently applied.
criteria.7-8: States assumptions about where the water goes, acknowledges rough estimates, and maintains mostly consistent causal logic.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, flags dependence on drain destination/geometry, and keeps all mechanisms mutually consistent.

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to.
items.original_question: 假设你做了“排干海洋”，并将水倒在好奇号火星车顶部，随着水的积累，火星会发生什么变化？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup and quantitative grounding
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response correctly frames the premise of transferring Earth's oceans to Mars and uses relevant orders of magnitude to constrain the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or ignores the amount of water involved; treats Mars as Earth-like without scale awareness.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges oceans are moved to Mars but gives little or incorrect quantitative context about volume, surface area, gravity, or basin depth.
criteria.5-6: Uses approximate ocean volume and Mars size/topography to estimate broad coverage, but with limited precision or weak linkage to consequences.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario with plausible estimates of water volume, global-equivalent depth, lowland filling, and Martian gravity/pressure constraints.
criteria.9-10: Integrates accurate order-of-magnitude calculations throughout, including ocean volume, Mars surface area, basin distribution, atmospheric implications, and physical limits.

criteria.name: Immediate physical behavior of water on Mars
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer explains what happens when huge amounts of liquid water arrive on cold, low-pressure Mars.
criteria.1-2: Claims the water simply forms stable Earth-like oceans with no discussion of pressure, temperature, boiling, freezing, or sublimation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions freezing or evaporation but treats processes simplistically or inconsistently with Martian conditions.
criteria.5-6: Explains that some water would boil, freeze, and alter local pressure, but omits major feedbacks or relative timescales.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent account of transient boiling, rapid cooling/freezing, vapor production, pressure increase, and eventual ice-covered bodies.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects phase behavior to Mars's low pressure, cold climate, latent heat, atmospheric thickening, ice insulation, and spatial variation over time.

criteria.name: Long-range atmospheric and climate consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the causal chain from added water to changes in Martian atmosphere, weather, greenhouse effects, and long-term stability.
criteria.1-2: Ignores atmospheric consequences or asserts Mars instantly becomes permanently habitable.
criteria.3-4: Mentions clouds or greenhouse warming but without a defensible causal chain or with major contradictions.
criteria.5-6: Describes temporary atmospheric thickening and weather, but weakly handles escape, collapse, or long-term cooling.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible transient storms, precipitation/snow, greenhouse feedbacks, atmospheric loss, and eventual cold trapping of water.
criteria.9-10: Balances short-term warming and vapor/cloud effects against Mars's weak gravity, lack of magnetic field, CO2 limits, radiative balance, and long-term atmospheric escape/collapse.

criteria.name: Geological, hydrological, and planetary surface effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects on Martian terrain, erosion, impacts, mineral chemistry, ice caps, and possible ocean/ice distribution.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful surface consequences beyond saying Mars gets wet.
criteria.3-4: Mentions flooding or oceans but not erosion, basin filling, freezing patterns, or geology.
criteria.5-6: Covers several surface effects such as flooding, sediment transport, and ice formation, but with gaps in spatial or temporal coherence.
criteria.7-8: Describes major floods, lowland seas, erosion, sedimentation, chemical alteration, ice sheets, and changing shorelines over time.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent planetary evolution scenario linking topography, cratered terrain, regolith interaction, salts, ice mechanics, volcanism/geothermal exceptions, and long-term redistribution.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response maintains a logically consistent long-range counterfactual narrative while distinguishing robust conclusions from speculative ones.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, unsupported certainties, or impossible claims such as effortless terraforming or stable open oceans indefinitely.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible claims but mixes incompatible assumptions or fails to track timescales and dependencies.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with basic uncertainty language, but leaves important causal links vague or overstates habitability outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains consistent short-, medium-, and long-term stages; flags uncertain quantities and avoids common false conclusions.
criteria.9-10: Presents a tightly reasoned causal chain with explicit assumptions, timescale separation, uncertainty bounds, and careful handling of speculative biology/terraforming claims.

items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust.
items.original_question: 如果你想将一架飞机固定在地面上，使其无法起飞，那么绳子必须用什么材料制成？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Force Scale
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the scenario as a rope or tether attempting to restrain a large airplane during takeoff, with realistic force scales such as 747 engine thrust, aircraft mass, friction, and tension.
criteria.1-2: Misframes the scenario or treats the rope as magically able to hold the plane without considering forces.
criteria.3-4: Mentions thrust or rope tension but uses vague or clearly unrealistic force assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that engine thrust creates enormous rope tension and that ordinary ropes/anchors would fail.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible magnitudes for thrust, weight, friction, or tension and relates them to rope/anchor failure.
criteria.9-10: Accurately anchors the analysis in realistic aircraft-scale forces, including multi-engine thrust and the limits of rope, ground anchor, and attachment points.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Failure Modes
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores the major physical failure mechanisms: rope breaking, anchor tearing out, attachment point failing, plane structure damage, tire/brake/skid behavior, and possible rotation or instability.
criteria.1-2: Gives a single simplistic outcome with no physical failure mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one failure mode, such as the rope snapping, but ignores other likely weak points.
criteria.5-6: Covers two or three plausible failure modes, though some are shallow or incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Explains several interacting failure modes, including rope strength, anchor strength, and aircraft attachment limits.
criteria.9-10: Comprehensively compares likely weak links and explains how different rope/anchor choices change whether the rope snaps, the anchor fails, or the plane is damaged.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the continuity and plausibility of the event sequence from engine spool-up and initial acceleration through tension buildup, structural response, possible ground motion, and final outcome.
criteria.1-2: Presents events in an incoherent or physically impossible order.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but skips key transitions or relies on unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly plausible short chain from thrust to rope/anchor failure.
criteria.7-8: Traces a coherent multi-stage chain including acceleration, tension growth, weak-link failure, and immediate consequences.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a detailed, causally consistent chain across short- and longer-term effects, including what happens if the tether briefly holds versus fails quickly.

criteria.name: Plausibility Under Variants and Boundary Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer calibrates outcomes for different versions of the premise, such as a hand-held rope, a rope tied to a truck or concrete anchor, an extremely strong cable, or different aircraft sizes.
criteria.1-2: Assumes one outcome applies universally regardless of rope, anchor, or aircraft.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges variants but treats them superficially or inconsistently.
criteria.5-6: Distinguishes ordinary rope from stronger anchoring in a basic way.
criteria.7-8: Explains how outcomes vary with rope strength, anchor mass, attachment location, runway friction, and airplane type.
criteria.9-10: Carefully bounds conclusions across realistic and extreme cases, noting when the limiting factor shifts from rope to anchor to aircraft structure or landing gear.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids internal contradictions and clearly separates confident conclusions from estimates or speculative effects in this airplane-tether counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as saying the rope both holds easily and snaps immediately, with no explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes some inconsistent claims or overconfident unsupported numerical statements.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent and expresses uncertainty for at least some estimates.
criteria.7-8: Maintains internal consistency and qualifies uncertain quantities such as rope rating, anchor capacity, and aircraft model.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes robust conclusions from parameter-dependent ones, avoids false precision, and resolves apparent conflicts between thrust, friction, structural limits, and tether behavior.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in.
items.original_question: 如果一座巨大的山峰（比如麦金利山）的底部一英寸消失了怎么办？山体下降1英寸的影响会发生什么？ 1英尺呢？如果山脚升高到山顶现在的高度，然后让整个山落到地上怎么办？

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?

criteria.name: Initial mechanical response and gap-closure timing
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise that the bottom inch of a massive mountain vanishes to the immediate gravitational drop, including the approximate timescale for the one-inch gap to close.
criteria.1-2: Claims the mountain floats, explodes instantly, or otherwise ignores gravity and gap closure.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes downward motion but gives an implausible or unsupported timescale.
criteria.5-6: Identifies rapid collapse of the one-inch gap but lacks quantitative reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Gives a plausible free-fall estimate near 70 ms with minor caveats or omissions.
criteria.9-10: Correctly explains free-fall closure of one inch in about 70 ms and notes the extreme danger of anything in the gap.

criteria.name: Causal fidelity to the counterfactual premise
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer stays faithful to the exact scenario: only the bottom inch vanishes beneath a massive mountain, rather than changing the amount, location, or physical assumptions without justification.
criteria.1-2: Replaces the premise with a different event, such as the whole mountain disappearing or levitating.
criteria.3-4: Frequently drifts from the one-inch removal premise or invents unsupported conditions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly keeps the premise but occasionally exaggerates or alters the geometry.
criteria.7-8: Maintains the one-inch basal void premise and reasons from it consistently.
criteria.9-10: Strictly preserves the premise while explicitly handling idealizations such as support, terrain contact, and material continuity.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage of stress, impact, and deformation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the physical mechanisms following gap closure, including impact, compression waves, fracturing, landslides, and redistribution of stresses through the mountain.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only a vague collapse with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impact or shaking but omits stress propagation and deformation.
criteria.5-6: Covers impact and some cracking or settling, but mechanisms are shallow.
criteria.7-8: Explains impact, stress waves, fracture, local crushing, and possible slope failures.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent multi-mechanism account including free fall, impact deceleration, seismic waves, rock failure, and uneven settling.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and scale calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly extends the immediate event into later consequences without overstating global effects, considering local seismic shaking, dust, avalanches, infrastructure damage, and stabilization.
criteria.1-2: Predicts absurd global catastrophe or no aftermath at all.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but with severe scale errors, such as planetwide destruction.
criteria.5-6: Mentions some local aftermath but lacks scale discipline or sequencing.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly describes local-to-regional shaking, rockfalls, dust, and damage over seconds to days.
criteria.9-10: Clearly sequences immediate closure, impact, seismic response, landslides, structural damage, aftershocks, and eventual settling with realistic scale limits.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes robust conclusions from assumptions, avoids internal contradictions, and handles unknowns such as mountain shape, rock strength, and contact conditions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident contradictory claims or impossible statements.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but contains major contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges unknowns but mixes firm and speculative claims inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Separates reliable conclusions from scenario-dependent outcomes with few contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, states assumptions, avoids contradictions, and preserves the robust conclusion that the gap closes in roughly 70 ms.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up.
items.original_question: 如果航天器使用火星天空起重机等火箭助推器在重返大气层时减速至每小时几英里会怎么样？它会消除对隔热罩的需要吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?

criteria.name: Orbital Mechanics and Core Counterfactual Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly identifies what it would mean for a spacecraft to slow to a few miles per hour during reentry, especially the distinction between altitude, orbital velocity, and falling from orbit.
criteria.1-2: Treats reentry as simply descending from height and misses that orbit is mostly sideways speed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions slowing down but poorly explains orbital velocity or confuses vertical and horizontal motion.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that orbital speed must be removed, but gives a partial or simplified account of the consequences.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that slowing to a few mph means canceling nearly all orbital velocity and transitioning to near-vertical descent.
criteria.9-10: Precisely connects the premise to orbital energy, deorbiting, loss of lift/trajectory, and why 'space is not hard because it is high up.'

criteria.name: Propulsion, Delta-v, and Propellant Feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer reasons through the rocket requirements needed to slow a spacecraft from orbital speed to a few miles per hour before or during reentry.
criteria.1-2: Ignores rocket requirements or implies small thrusters could easily do it.
criteria.3-4: Notes it would require fuel but gives no meaningful scale or mechanism.
criteria.5-6: Identifies very large delta-v and propellant needs, with some explanation of why this is impractical.
criteria.7-8: Explains that canceling orbital velocity needs roughly orbit-insertion-scale delta-v and large propellant mass.
criteria.9-10: Uses rocket-equation-style reasoning or equivalent scaling to show why the vehicle becomes dominated by propellant and mission architecture changes radically.

criteria.name: Atmospheric Entry, Heating, and Descent Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how the counterfactual affects reentry heating, drag, descent time, terminal velocity, and landing dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Claims the spacecraft would simply drift gently down without addressing gravity, drag, or heating.
criteria.3-4: Mentions less heating but misses that gravity would rapidly accelerate the vehicle again.
criteria.5-6: Explains reduced initial heating and notes the craft would still fall and accelerate through the atmosphere.
criteria.7-8: Connects low-speed entry to lower shock heating, longer powered/ballistic descent, terminal velocity, and need for landing systems.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent atmospheric sequence from near-stationary high-altitude descent through acceleration, drag buildup, possible heating regimes, and final landing constraints.

criteria.name: Long-Range Engineering and Mission-Level Implications
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows downstream effects on spacecraft design, launch mass, thermal protection, structure, guidance, safety, and comparison to existing reentry methods.
criteria.1-2: Focuses on only one immediate effect and ignores broader design implications.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but without causal connection to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Covers several implications such as fuel, heat shield reduction, and landing method, but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Links propulsion choice to mass, launch cost, TPS tradeoffs, guidance, and landing architecture.
criteria.9-10: Provides an integrated mission-level analysis showing why conventional aerobraking is preferred despite heating, and when powered descent might make sense.

criteria.name: Causal Coherence, Contradiction Control, and Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response maintains a consistent causal chain, avoids contradictions, and appropriately qualifies uncertain details under the counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as saying it both remains in orbit and stops relative to Earth without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct pieces but inconsistent sequencing or unsupported absolute claims.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor gaps or overconfident simplifications.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal chain and flags assumptions such as where the slowing occurs and vehicle shape.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes scenarios, frames uncertainties quantitatively or conditionally, and avoids misleading claims while preserving the central conclusion.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ...
items.original_question: 如果您有整个（例如英文）维基百科的印刷版本，您需要多少台打印机才能跟上对实时版本所做的更改？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity: live paper Wikipedia
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the scenario as trying to keep a printed English Wikipedia synchronized with ongoing real-time changes, rather than merely printing one static copy.
criteria.1-2: Treats the task only as a one-time printout or ignores real-time updating entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions updates but mostly analyzes a static Wikipedia print job.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes both initial printing and live updating, but blurs which quantities apply to each.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes the initial corpus from the continuing edit stream and reasons from that premise.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the live-updating premise throughout, including revisions, additions, deletions, and synchronization limits.

criteria.name: Quantitative plausibility of printer-load estimates
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer gives plausible order-of-magnitude estimates for Wikipedia size, edit rate, page yield, printer speed, and the resulting number of printers needed.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful numbers or gives wildly impossible estimates.
criteria.3-4: Uses some numbers but with major scale errors, such as confusing articles, pages, bytes, and edits.
criteria.5-6: Gives rough estimates with partially plausible magnitudes but weak justification.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable assumptions for edit volume, page counts, and printer throughput to reach a defensible estimate.
criteria.9-10: Builds a transparent order-of-magnitude calculation and calibrates the 'surprisingly few printers' conclusion appropriately.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage: what the printers would actually print
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the operational mechanisms involved in printing a live Wikipedia, including full pages versus diffs, reprints after edits, formatting, queues, and update conflicts.
criteria.1-2: Does not explain what is being printed or how updates are handled.
criteria.3-4: Assumes pages simply appear on paper without addressing revisions or formatting.
criteria.5-6: Mentions edits or reprints but omits important mechanics such as diffs, queues, or replaced pages.
criteria.7-8: Explains how article changes translate into printed output and identifies major workflow choices.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly analyzes full-page reprints versus diffs, edit bursts, deletion/rollback behavior, formatting overhead, and synchronization failures.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and bottlenecks
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces consequences beyond printer count, such as paper consumption, ink/toner, storage, sorting, energy, labor, waste, and physical usability.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a superficial answer with no downstream effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two consequences without causal development.
criteria.5-6: Covers several practical issues but treats them as disconnected facts.
criteria.7-8: Connects printer output to paper supply, storage growth, replacement pages, logistics, and human handling.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent long-range causal chain from edit stream to material throughput, waste accumulation, archival disorder, and eventual impracticality.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertainty in Wikipedia statistics and printer assumptions while avoiding internal contradictions about scale, timing, or feasibility.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but unsupported claims and contradicts itself on basic feasibility.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty vaguely but still contains major inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Uses caveats and mostly consistent reasoning, though some assumptions conflict.
criteria.7-8: States assumptions, gives ranges or approximations, and keeps the causal story internally consistent.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates estimates, flags dependence on definitions and dates, and avoids contradictions across all quantitative and qualitative claims.
