rubrics.question_focus: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?

criteria.name: Buoyancy and scale physics under the helium-balloon premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about whether helium tanks plus a giant balloon could meaningfully reduce a falling person's speed, including buoyant force, required balloon volume, mass of equipment, and why ordinary party-balloon intuition fails.
criteria.1-2: Claims helium tanks or a modest balloon would simply make the jumper float or be safe, with little or no physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions buoyancy or terminal velocity but gives mostly qualitative or incorrect scale estimates.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes a very large balloon is needed and that tank mass matters, but leaves key force/volume tradeoffs vague.
criteria.7-8: Explains buoyancy versus weight and drag, notes enormous volume requirements, tank penalties, and reduced terminal velocity plausibly.
criteria.9-10: Gives coherent order-of-magnitude reasoning for helium volume, lift, drag, payload mass, and why feasibility is marginal but not magical.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain from aircraft exit to landing
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response traces the full sequence of events after jumping from a plane: exit conditions, initial acceleration, balloon deployment or inflation, changing descent rate, stability, drift, and final touchdown.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on one moment, such as jumping or landing, without a causal sequence.
criteria.3-4: Provides a simple sequence but skips major phases like deployment timing or landing dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Covers fall, balloon effect, and landing, but with weak links between phases or unrealistic transitions.
criteria.7-8: Builds a mostly coherent timeline including freefall, inflation/deployment challenges, slowing, wind drift, and impact speed.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a detailed, physically consistent chain across all phases, including how earlier choices affect later survival odds.

criteria.name: Practical engineering constraints of tanks, balloon, and deployment
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for real-world feasibility issues: carrying high-pressure helium tanks, regulator flow rate, balloon material strength, inflation time, tangling, tearing, cold/low-pressure air, and whether pre-inflation or midair inflation is plausible.
criteria.1-2: Ignores engineering constraints and treats the setup as effortless.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that it would be hard to build but gives no specific obstacles.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some practical problems, such as tank weight or inflation time, but omits several critical ones.
criteria.7-8: Discusses multiple constraints, including tank mass, deployment, material strength, and midair instability.
criteria.9-10: Integrates engineering limits quantitatively or causally, distinguishing impossible, barely plausible, and safer design variants.

criteria.name: Human survival factors and environmental hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer considers biological and safety consequences beyond the balloon physics, including altitude, oxygen deprivation, cold, aircraft-exit trauma, acceleration loads, spinning, collision with the balloon, and survivable landing speeds.
criteria.1-2: States survival or death without considering human physiological limits.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger generally but misses most specific hazards.
criteria.5-6: Covers a few hazards such as hypoxia or impact speed, but does not connect them to the scenario.
criteria.7-8: Explains several relevant risks and how balloon size, descent rate, and altitude affect survivability.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced survival assessment across altitude, deployment, descent, drift, and landing, with realistic thresholds or comparisons.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer avoids overconfident or self-contradictory claims while clearly separating what is physically possible, what is practically unlikely, and what would require extreme assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Is internally contradictory or presents fantasy outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Uses some hedging but still makes unsupported absolute claims or inconsistent statements.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but contains minor contradictions or poorly calibrated confidence.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions, uncertainty, and conditional outcomes with few contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes theoretical possibility from practical feasibility, flags unknowns, and keeps all causal claims mutually consistent.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure.
items.original_question: 如果所有数字数据都存储在打孔卡上，谷歌的数据仓库有多大？

rubrics.question_focus: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity and scale recognition
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently accepts the premise that all digital data must be stored on physical punch cards and correctly reasons about the enormous scale of modern digital storage, especially relative to large organizations such as Google.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the punch-card premise, or treats punch cards as roughly equivalent to modern storage.
criteria.3-4: Mentions punch cards but severely underestimates the scale of global or organizational data storage.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that punch cards would be vastly larger and less efficient than modern storage, but gives only rough or incomplete scale reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains the extreme physical scale, storage density limits, and logistical burden implied by storing modern digital data on punch cards.
criteria.9-10: Provides highly coherent scale reasoning, including approximate comparisons, uncertainty about exact data volumes, and implications for entities like Google or global data centers.

criteria.name: Mechanistic coverage of storage, retrieval, and computation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the mechanisms by which punch-card storage would affect writing, indexing, retrieving, copying, processing, and transmitting digital information.
criteria.1-2: Provides vague claims about inconvenience without explaining mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Discusses one or two mechanisms, such as storage bulk or slow reading, but omits most core operations.
criteria.5-6: Covers several mechanisms including physical storage, retrieval speed, and copying, but lacks depth or interconnection.
criteria.7-8: Explains how punch cards would constrain indexing, random access, duplication, error handling, computation, and networking.
criteria.9-10: Gives a detailed, causally linked account of the entire data lifecycle under punch-card storage, including bottlenecks in search, backups, versioning, and machine processing.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects on technology, economy, and society
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible long-range consequences for computing infrastructure, internet services, scientific research, business models, labor, land use, and everyday digital life.
criteria.1-2: Lists superficial effects with little connection to the premise.
criteria.3-4: Identifies a few obvious effects, such as slower computers or larger warehouses, but does not develop consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains several downstream effects on technology and daily life, though chains are short or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Traces coherent multi-step impacts on cloud computing, search, streaming, AI, finance, research, and physical infrastructure.
criteria.9-10: Builds rich long-range causal chains showing how punch-card storage would reshape industries, institutions, labor systems, environmental demands, and the feasibility of modern digital society.

criteria.name: Plausibility, quantitative calibration, and uncertainty handling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses plausible estimates and calibrated uncertainty rather than unsupported precision, especially for unknown quantities such as Google’s total storage capacity.
criteria.1-2: Makes implausible or wildly precise claims without justification.
criteria.3-4: Uses rough numbers or comparisons but with major errors or no uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and gives broadly plausible estimates, but calculations or comparisons are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable order-of-magnitude reasoning for punch-card capacity, physical volume, weight, or throughput, while noting uncertainty.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates estimates, avoids false precision, distinguishes known from speculative claims, and uses quantitative reasoning to support rather than overstate conclusions.

criteria.name: Contradiction control and consistency of the counterfactual world
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids internal contradictions, such as relying on modern dense digital storage while claiming all digital data is on punch cards, and maintains a coherent technological environment.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions that undermine the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Often violates the premise by assuming ordinary hard drives, flash memory, or cloud storage still hold digital data.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise but includes some inconsistent assumptions or unexplained exceptions.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent punch-card-based world and explains any necessary auxiliary technologies without contradicting the premise.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a fully coherent counterfactual system, explicitly manages edge cases such as RAM, caches, transmission, backups, and analog machinery, and avoids hidden reliance on modern digital storage.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and ascent kinematics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly applies the premise of continuously rising vertically at one foot per second and uses that rate to anchor consequences over seconds, minutes, hours, and longer.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats the ascent as fast, powered flight, falling, or teleportation.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes upward motion but gives few or incorrect time-height estimates.
criteria.5-6: Uses the 1 ft/s rate for some milestones, with minor numerical or scale errors.
criteria.7-8: Accurately maps key heights to times, such as arms' reach, buildings, clouds, and cruising altitude.
criteria.9-10: Consistently grounds the whole causal chain in precise 1 ft/s timing and altitude scales.

criteria.name: Near-ground and human-scale consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of immediate effects after lift-off, including rescue difficulty, collision risks, clothing/equipment needs, and interaction with nearby structures or people.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the first minutes or invents implausible immediate disasters.
criteria.3-4: Mentions leaving reach but misses practical rescue and obstacle issues.
criteria.5-6: Covers basic near-ground outcomes, such as being grabbed, needing help, or hitting buildings.
criteria.7-8: Explains escalating rescue difficulty, rooftop/crane limits, wind drift, and object collision hazards.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent near-ground sequence with realistic timing, rescue options, and environmental complications.

criteria.name: Atmospheric, physiological, and thermal mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly explains how altitude affects temperature, pressure, oxygen availability, wind, clouds, and survivability during the slow ascent.
criteria.1-2: Shows little understanding of atmosphere or human physiology.
criteria.3-4: Mentions cold or oxygen vaguely but with major errors.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several relevant hazards, such as cold, hypoxia, low pressure, and weather.
criteria.7-8: Connects hazards to approximate altitude and time ranges with mostly correct mechanisms.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates temperature lapse rate, hypoxia, pressure effects, wind/weather, exposure, and likely death without protection.

criteria.name: Long-range chain coherence across altitude regimes
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows consequences beyond the lower atmosphere, including aircraft altitude, stratosphere, near-space, and whether orbital or escape outcomes are treated correctly.
criteria.1-2: Stops early or jumps to space with no coherent transition.
criteria.3-4: Lists high-altitude events but in confused or contradictory order.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible broad sequence but omits major regimes or has scale mistakes.
criteria.7-8: Tracks the ascent through aviation altitudes, lethal atmosphere, stratosphere, and near-space with good continuity.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a rigorous long-range causal chain, including why slow vertical ascent does not imply stable orbit or escape by itself.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes assumptions from known outcomes, avoids internal contradictions, and handles ambiguities such as source of lift, wind drift, equipment, and rescue attempts.

criteria.3-4: Has several unsupported claims or inconsistent assumptions about motion, survival, or environment.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies.
items.original_question: 如果风速达到 500 英里/小时，它会卷起人吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?

criteria.name: Wind-speed physics and force scaling

criteria.1-2: Treats 500 mph wind like ordinary strong wind or uses clearly false physics.
criteria.3-4: Notes it is extremely destructive but gives little or incorrect force scaling.
criteria.5-6: Correctly links damage to drag increasing with velocity squared, with rough qualitative scale.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible quantitative estimates or comparisons, such as EF5 tornado-scale forces and lethal debris speeds.
criteria.9-10: Accurately applies dynamic pressure, drag, density, and exposure limits while avoiding exaggerated effects like instant planetary destruction.

criteria.name: Immediate effects on humans, objects, and structures
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage and plausibility of near-term consequences for people, vehicles, buildings, trees, and loose debris in 500 mph winds.

criteria.3-4: Mentions destruction but omits key hazards like debris impact, structural failure, or inability to stand.
criteria.5-6: Explains that exposed humans would be killed or severely injured and many structures and vehicles would fail.
criteria.7-8: Covers debris projectiles, building-envelope failure, roof/wall collapse, vehicle displacement, and tree stripping.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent, mechanism-based account of how exposure, anchoring, shape, shelter, and duration determine survival and damage.

criteria.name: Environmental and geographic downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates reasoning about broader effects depending on whether 500 mph winds occur over land, ocean, cities, forests, or coastlines.
criteria.1-2: Ignores location and treats all settings identically.
criteria.3-4: Mentions broad devastation but gives little environment-specific reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some major downstream effects such as deforestation, erosion, waves, or urban debris fields.
criteria.7-8: Differentiates land and ocean outcomes, including storm surge/waves, salt spray, soil stripping, crop loss, and infrastructure disruption.
criteria.9-10: Traces long-range cascading effects across ecosystems, coastlines, power grids, transport, water systems, and recovery conditions without overclaiming.

criteria.name: Counterfactual chain coherence and timescale control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a logical sequence from the wind event through immediate, secondary, and longer-term consequences.
criteria.1-2: Jumps between unrelated outcomes or contradicts the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose sequence but mixes immediate and long-term effects confusingly.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent chain from wind forces to damage to aftermath.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates seconds/minutes, hours/days, and weeks/months effects with plausible causal links.
criteria.9-10: Builds a robust long-range causal chain including feedbacks, dependencies, and limiting conditions such as storm size and duration.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction avoidance
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer states assumptions, handles ambiguity in the question, and avoids unsupported or contradictory claims.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute, sensational claims with no assumptions or contains major contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges little uncertainty and overstates several effects.
criteria.5-6: Notes that outcomes depend on duration, area, terrain, and shelter, but not consistently.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates claims well, distinguishing likely, possible, and unlikely effects under different scenarios.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly frames assumptions about wind duration, spatial scale, altitude, and environment, while keeping all conclusions physically consistent.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one.
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Physical Feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines a coherent tiny-but-ultra-massive asteroid scenario and respects constraints from density, radius, mass, and possible gravitational collapse.
criteria.1-2: Treats the asteroid like an ordinary rock or planet without addressing the tiny/high-mass premise.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges unusual mass or gravity but leaves the setup vague or physically inconsistent.
criteria.5-6: Uses a plausible assumed size/mass or surface gravity, with limited discussion of extreme density constraints.
criteria.7-8: Clearly parameterizes the scenario and notes feasibility limits such as exotic density or collapse risk.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames multiple viable regimes, including black-hole/Schwarzschild or material-strength limits where relevant.

criteria.name: Gravity, Tides, and Local Surface Mechanics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates explanation of how gravity behaves on a very small massive body, including steep gradients, walking, falling, horizon effects, and orientation changes.
criteria.1-2: Gives generic high-gravity claims with little connection to tiny radius effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions strong gravity but misses gradients, curvature, or local motion consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains surface gravity and some effects of small radius, such as rapid horizon curvature.
criteria.7-8: Covers gravity gradients, tidal forces across the body, changing down-direction, and difficult surface movement.
criteria.9-10: Integrates surface gravity, curvature, tidal variation, and body-scale mechanics into a coherent lived experience.

criteria.name: Escape Velocity, Orbits, and Motion Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons that a tiny body can have high surface gravity yet relatively low escape velocity, producing unusual jumping, throwing, and orbital effects.
criteria.1-2: Assumes high gravity always means impossible escape or ignores escape/orbital mechanics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions jumping or escape but confuses gravity, mass, radius, and velocity relationships.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that escape speed depends on radius as well as gravity and gives plausible consequences.
criteria.7-8: Explains low escape velocity, close orbits, short orbital paths, and hazards from jumping or thrown objects.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively or semi-quantitatively connects radius, surface gravity, escape speed, orbital period, and practical motion outcomes.

criteria.name: Habitability and Downstream Survival Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of major consequences for a human living there, including atmosphere retention, pressure, radiation, landing, structural stability, and biological stress.
criteria.1-2: Focuses on spectacle while ignoring whether a human could survive.
criteria.3-4: Mentions survival problems but only in a generic or disconnected way.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant issues such as atmosphere loss, extreme gravity gradients, or landing hazards.
criteria.7-8: Connects physical mechanics to breathing, movement, shelter, transport, and environmental protection.
criteria.9-10: Provides a broad, causally linked survival analysis including atmosphere, tides, engineering constraints, radiation/thermal exposure, and logistics.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent chain from the counterfactual premise through near-term and long-term effects while clearly marking assumptions and uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or unsupported leaps that break the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with assumptions stated in broad terms and only minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Builds a clear causal chain and distinguishes likely effects from parameter-dependent ones.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous consistency across all consequences, explicitly calibrating uncertainty and alternative outcomes by asteroid size, mass, and density.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense.
items.original_question: 我心不在焉地搅拌着一杯热茶，心里想：我这不是给杯子里加了动能吗？我知道搅拌确实有助于冷却茶，但如果我搅拌得更快怎么办？我可以通过搅拌来煮一杯水吗？

rubrics.question_focus: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?

criteria.name: Endpoint Plausibility for Stirring-to-Boiling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically plausible bottom line for whether stirring water could make it boil, distinguishing theoretical possibility from practical feasibility.
criteria.1-2: Gives a clearly false endpoint, such as saying ordinary stirring can easily boil water or that stirring cannot add heat at all.
criteria.3-4: Has a partially correct endpoint but misses the key theory-versus-practice distinction.
criteria.5-6: States that stirring can add heat but is practically insufficient, with limited qualification.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that boiling by stirring is possible in principle but not feasible by normal human stirring due to power and losses.
criteria.9-10: Gives a precise, well-qualified conclusion: mechanical work can become heat and eventually boil water only under extreme or engineered conditions, not ordinary stirring.

criteria.name: Mechanism of Energy Conversion
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the causal mechanism from stirring to molecular heating: work input, fluid motion, viscosity, turbulence, and dissipation into thermal energy.
criteria.1-2: Omits or denies the mechanism by which stirring energy can become heat.
criteria.3-4: Mentions friction or energy vaguely without connecting it to water temperature rise.
criteria.5-6: Explains that mechanical work is converted to heat through friction or viscosity, but with shallow detail.
criteria.7-8: Describes stirring work, turbulence/viscous dissipation, and molecular thermal energy coherently.
criteria.9-10: Provides a complete causal account from applied torque to fluid motion, viscous dissipation, thermalization, and temperature increase.

criteria.name: Quantitative Scale and Practical Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures the scale of energy and power required to heat water to boiling compared with realistic stirring power.
criteria.1-2: Ignores scale entirely or implies negligible effort is enough.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes it would take a lot of energy but gives no meaningful sense of magnitude.
criteria.5-6: Notes that heating water requires substantial energy and human stirring power is too low.
criteria.7-8: Uses approximate numbers or comparisons, such as heat capacity, watts of stirring power, and long timescales.
criteria.9-10: Accurately estimates energy/power needs, compares them to human/mechanical stirring, and accounts for why practical boiling is unrealistic.

criteria.name: Long-Range Thermal Chain and Losses
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows the downstream consequences after stirring begins, including heat accumulation, environmental losses, evaporation, and boiling conditions.
criteria.1-2: Treats boiling as an immediate result of motion without considering temperature, losses, or phase change.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heating but not the full path to boiling or the role of losses.
criteria.5-6: Connects stirring to gradual heating and notes some heat loss to surroundings.
criteria.7-8: Explains that sustained input must exceed losses and raise the whole sample to the boiling point before vigorous boiling occurs.
criteria.9-10: Coherently traces the full chain: work input, heat buildup, losses to container/air, evaporation, boiling-point conditions, and steady-state limits.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids internal contradictions and uses appropriate caveats about assumptions such as insulation, container size, pressure, and stirring device.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as saying stirring both cannot heat water and can boil it easily.
criteria.3-4: Has confusing or inconsistent claims about feasibility, energy conservation, or boiling.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but leaves important assumptions unstated or overgeneralizes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent answer with clear caveats about ordinary versus idealized conditions.
criteria.9-10: Is internally consistent and carefully calibrated, specifying assumptions about insulation, ambient pressure, water volume, and available stirring power.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it.
items.original_question: 距离超新星有多近才能获得致命剂量的中微子辐射？

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling: lethal neutrino dose from a nearby supernova
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly accepts the counterfactual while acknowledging why it is physically unusual: neutrinos interact extremely weakly, so a lethal dose requires an extraordinarily intense nearby supernova neutrino flux.
criteria.1-2: Treats neutrinos like ordinary radiation or ignores the lethal-neutrino premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions neutrinos weakly interact but gives confused or inconsistent implications.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the premise is extreme and explains weak interaction in broad terms.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains why lethality requires immense flux and keeps the counterfactual consistent.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the premise as rare/extreme, distinguishes real physics from assumption, and reasons from it without handwaving.

criteria.name: Mechanism of biological and physical damage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of how lethal neutrino radiation would harm Earth life and matter, including rare neutrino interactions, energy deposition, internal irradiation, tissue damage, and possible whole-planet dose effects.
criteria.1-2: Gives vague destruction with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions radiation sickness or death but not how neutrinos cause it.
criteria.5-6: Explains that neutrino interactions deposit energy in bodies and tissues.
criteria.7-8: Connects interaction rate, dose, DNA/cellular damage, and rapid biological mortality.
criteria.9-10: Covers organism-level, ecosystem-level, and material/geophysical implications of intense neutrino energy deposition with appropriate caveats.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain after the event
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces coherent downstream consequences beyond the initial neutrino flash, including immediate mortality, ecological collapse, atmospheric/oceanic effects, infrastructure failure, and planetary recovery or sterilization scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Only states everyone dies or Earth explodes with no chain.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few effects but with little timing or causal order.
criteria.5-6: Provides a basic sequence from neutrino exposure to mass death and ecosystem disruption.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible timeline from minutes/hours through years, covering biosphere and civilization effects.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust multi-stage causal chain, including feedbacks, survivors if any, collapse dynamics, and long-term planetary consequences.

criteria.name: Integration with other supernova hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes neutrino radiation from accompanying supernova effects such as gamma rays, X-rays, cosmic rays, ejecta, ozone depletion, heating, and gravitational effects, without letting them contradict the neutrino-centered premise.
criteria.1-2: Confuses neutrinos with blast waves, fire, or gravity throughout.
criteria.3-4: Mentions other supernova dangers but muddles their timing or relevance.
criteria.5-6: Separates neutrinos from photons, particles, and ejecta in a basic way.
criteria.7-8: Explains relative timing and likely importance of neutrinos versus later radiation/cosmic-ray hazards.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates all major supernova hazards while preserving the specified lethal-neutrino counterfactual as the driving event.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, flags dependence on distance, supernova type, neutrino energy, dose threshold, and shielding assumptions, and avoids internal contradictions such as neutrinos being both harmless and instantly explosive without explanation.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims or contradicts itself repeatedly.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but includes major unsupported or conflicting claims.
criteria.5-6: Notes key unknowns such as distance or dose while maintaining a mostly consistent answer.
criteria.7-8: Carefully qualifies estimates and keeps assumptions, mechanisms, and outcomes aligned.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly tracks assumptions and uncertainty ranges, resolves apparent paradoxes, and maintains consistency across the full counterfactual scenario.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Interpretation and Quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as humans continuing the linear height-growth velocity typical of a one-month-old infant, rather than merely being newborn-sized or growing exponentially without justification.

criteria.7-8: Clearly estimates continued linear height growth from newborn/one-month infant rates and gives plausible adult-scale outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Precisely defines the assumed rate, distinguishes linear from exponential growth, and transparently calculates heights across key ages.

criteria.name: Biophysical Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains the biological and physical mechanisms that would limit or be affected by indefinite infant-rate growth, especially square-cube scaling, bones, muscles, circulation, metabolism, and organ function.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only that people would be tall, with no mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Includes one or two superficial effects such as needing more food or being heavy.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant mechanisms but misses major constraints like square-cube law or cardiovascular load.

criteria.9-10: Integrates biological growth regulation with physics-based scaling and explains which systems fail first and why.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence

criteria.1-2: Provides isolated claims with no temporal or causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Gives a short-term consequence only, such as becoming very tall as adults.
criteria.5-6: Discusses adult outcomes and some downstream effects but with gaps or weak sequencing.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain from childhood growth to adult physiology, buildings, transport, food demand, and medicine.
criteria.9-10: Shows a robust multi-stage trajectory, including feedback effects on survival, reproduction, economy, design standards, and population sustainability.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty, and Assumption Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer calibrates uncertainty around infant growth rates, biological feasibility, and whether natural selection or medical intervention could sustain such bodies.
criteria.1-2: Presents implausible certainties or fantasy claims without qualification.
criteria.3-4: Uses vague qualifiers but does not identify uncertain assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges some uncertainty in growth rates or survivability but does not bound estimates.
criteria.7-8: States assumptions, gives approximate ranges, and separates calculable height from speculative survival outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Carefully bounds numerical estimates, flags model limits, and distinguishes counterfactual biology from real human developmental constraints.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids contradictions such as saying humans both remain normal-sized and grow continuously, or invoking impossible physiology without noting counterfactual changes.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions that undermine the answer.
criteria.3-4: Has several inconsistent claims about growth rate, final size, or survival.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but includes some unsupported leaps or conflicting estimates.
criteria.7-8: Maintains consistent assumptions and aligns numerical estimates with biological consequences.
criteria.9-10: Is internally rigorous throughout, with all consequences following from the same stated growth model and no unresolved contradictions.

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity for a T. rex in Modern NYC

criteria.name: Biological and Physical Plausibility

criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but also contains major inconsistencies or unsupported certainties.
criteria.5-6: Generally consistent, with limited caveats about uncertain behavior and response timing.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while avoiding contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty throughout, compares scenarios, explains key sensitivities, and keeps all causal claims mutually consistent.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?

criteria.name: Magnitude and dilution of all the world's tea in the Great Lakes
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly estimates or qualitatively frames the amount of tea relative to the enormous volume of the Great Lakes, leading to the central conclusion that the resulting concentration would be extremely weak.

criteria.name: Chemical and physical mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains what actually happens when tea leaves or brewed tea enter the lakes, including extraction, mixing, settling, degradation, and the fate of caffeine, tannins, pigments, and organic matter.

criteria.9-10: Provides a well-integrated account of extraction limits, lake mixing times, suspended solids, dissolved organics, caffeine/tannin fate, and microbial breakdown.

criteria.name: Ecological and water-quality downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces environmental consequences for the Great Lakes, including nutrient/organic loading, oxygen demand, turbidity, microbial activity, aquatic life, and shoreline impacts.
criteria.1-2: Claims either no effect or catastrophic ecosystem collapse without justification.
criteria.3-4: Lists vague environmental effects but does not connect them to tea concentration or lake processes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible impacts, such as organic matter decomposition or temporary water discoloration, but lacks depth.
criteria.7-8: Connects organic loading, microbial decomposition, oxygen demand, turbidity, and localized biological impacts to dilution and mixing.
criteria.9-10: Gives a calibrated account distinguishing lake-wide minor effects from potentially stronger local or short-term impacts near dumping sites, sediments, shorelines, or water intakes.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent sequence from dumping through immediate mixing, short-term sensory and chemical changes, medium-term ecological processing, and longer-term flushing or sediment burial.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or jumps to outcomes that do not follow from the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose sequence but confuses timescales, causes, or endpoints.
criteria.5-6: Provides a basic timeline with some plausible stages but leaves gaps in causal transitions.
criteria.7-8: Develops a coherent multi-stage chain from input to dilution, processing, impacts, and eventual dissipation.
criteria.9-10: Tracks multiple interacting pathways over time, including uneven initial distribution, mixing times, biological processing, outflow, sedimentation, and recovery.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertain quantities and assumptions transparently while avoiding internal contradictions about whether the lakes become tea, remain mostly water, or suffer major impacts.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but unsupported claims and contradicts itself on concentration or effects.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially but still overstates outcomes or contains notable inconsistencies.
criteria.5-6: Uses reasonable hedging and mostly avoids contradictions, though assumptions are not always explicit.
criteria.7-8: States key assumptions, distinguishes order-of-magnitude estimates from certainties, and keeps conclusions consistent.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty around tea quantity, form of dumping, mixing, and ecological thresholds while maintaining a consistent, non-exaggerated conclusion.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV.
items.original_question: 如果世界上的所有病毒都集中到一个区域会怎样？它们会占据多少体积以及它们会是什么样子？

rubrics.question_focus: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity and scale reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as physically concentrating all viruses on Earth and reasons about the resulting scale, composition, and immediate implications without drifting into unrelated scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats viruses as large organisms, magic, or a guaranteed instant apocalypse.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes viruses are gathered but gives vague or exaggerated scale claims with little grounding.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the pile would be enormous in number but limited in physical volume/mass, with some basic scale awareness.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes viral abundance from physical size and notes that most viruses are not human pathogens.
criteria.9-10: Accurately frames the pile as vast in count, modest relative to macroscopic matter, dominated by non-human/environmental viruses, and carefully follows the exact premise.

criteria.name: Coverage of viral diversity and host specificity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for the fact that Earth's viruses infect bacteria, archaea, plants, animals, fungi, and humans, with strong host specificity shaping the consequences.
criteria.1-2: Implies all viruses infect humans or all life equally.
criteria.3-4: Mentions multiple viruses but does not explain host specificity or relative abundance.
criteria.5-6: Notes that many viruses target non-human hosts, especially bacteria, but with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that bacteriophages and environmental viruses dominate and that human viruses are a tiny fraction.
criteria.9-10: Clearly describes viral diversity, host-range limits, ecological roles, and why concentrating all viruses would not make every virus a direct human threat.

criteria.name: Mechanistic analysis of infection risk and containment
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly explains what would happen biologically and physically if the viruses were concentrated, including viability, exposure routes, containment, and environmental conditions.
criteria.1-2: Claims infection occurs merely by proximity or that all viruses immediately activate.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger but lacks mechanisms such as transmission route, host contact, or survivability.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that risk depends on exposure, containment, and whether viruses remain viable.
criteria.7-8: Explains mechanisms such as aerosolization, fluid contact, decay outside hosts, UV/heat sensitivity, and biosecurity needs.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced mechanism-based risk assessment distinguishing contained versus dispersed piles, viable versus degraded virions, and pathogen-specific transmission constraints.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream ecological and societal consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces coherent downstream effects beyond the initial pile, including ecological disruption, disease risk, research implications, and possible global responses.
criteria.1-2: Gives only a one-step outcome with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Lists consequences such as disease or panic without causal links.
criteria.5-6: Describes some plausible effects, such as quarantine, research value, or ecological disturbance.
criteria.7-8: Connects concentration/removal of viruses to effects on microbial populations, ecosystems, public health, and governance.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain covering containment response, biosafety, ecological consequences of removing/displacing viruses, disease risks if released, and scientific opportunities.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids unsupported certainty, handles unknowns such as exact viral biomass and viability, and remains internally consistent with known virology.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or confidently false claims, such as viruses being alive cells or all being deadly to humans.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct ideas but also overconfident or inconsistent statements.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with basic caveats about uncertainty but some imprecision.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language for estimates and unknowns while avoiding sensationalism.
criteria.9-10: Consistently distinguishes known facts, estimates, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradictions and explicitly qualifies uncertain quantities and scenarios.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth.
items.original_question: 有没有什么方法可以让枪射击后子弹飞到空中，然后可以安全地用手接住？例如射手位于海平面，捕手位于山上，位于枪的最远射程处。

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and endpoint plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly handles the premise of a bullet that has already slowed down and gives a plausible yes/no outcome for trying to catch it.
criteria.1-2: Treats the bullet as fully lethal regardless of speed or gives an unsupported absolute answer.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges speed matters but gives a vague or inconsistent conclusion about catchability.
criteria.5-6: States that catching may be possible only if the bullet is slow enough, but with limited explanation.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that a sufficiently slowed bullet could be caught while a still-fast one remains dangerous.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames catchability as dependent on velocity, mass, kinetic energy, and stopping distance, with a well-calibrated conclusion.

criteria.name: Mechanics of energy, momentum, and impulse
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains the physical mechanisms that determine injury or safe catching: kinetic energy, momentum, force, and time/distance over which the bullet is stopped.
criteria.1-2: Omits core mechanics or uses incorrect physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions speed or force but confuses energy, momentum, or impact severity.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that lower speed reduces danger but only partially explains why.
criteria.7-8: Explains kinetic energy and impulse well enough to distinguish a painful impact from penetration.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects speed reduction to energy loss, momentum transfer, stopping time, hand motion, and resulting force.

criteria.name: Mechanisms by which a bullet slows down
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how a fired bullet could become slow enough to catch, including air drag, long distance, water, soft materials, ricochet, or staged magic-trick methods.
criteria.1-2: Does not explain how the bullet slowed or assumes slowing happens magically.
criteria.3-4: Mentions slowing only generally, with little causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies at least one plausible slowing mechanism but leaves out important constraints.
criteria.7-8: Covers several realistic mechanisms and explains why they reduce velocity.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent account of realistic slowing pathways and distinguishes natural deceleration from staged or illusion-based bullet-catching tricks.

criteria.name: Long-range consequence chain and safety risks
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces downstream effects after slowing: impact on the hand, penetration risk, ricochet unpredictability, heat, spin, deformation, and practical safety concerns.
criteria.1-2: Ignores consequences or falsely presents the act as simply safe.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger but gives little detail about what could happen.
criteria.5-6: Covers basic risks such as bruising or penetration but misses several relevant effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple downstream risks and distinguishes controlled from uncontrolled situations.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent chain from slowed flight to contact, stopping, injury likelihood, object behavior, and why real attempts remain unsafe.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, resolves apparent contradictions with the bullet-catch magic trick, and keeps claims consistent with the counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, such as saying it is both impossible and routine without qualification.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but mixes incompatible claims or ignores the magic-trick context.
criteria.5-6: Generally consistent, but with weak caveats or unclear distinction between real and staged catching.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty well and explains that magic bullet catches are usually tricks or controlled setups.
criteria.9-10: Maintains full internal consistency, separates physics from performance illusion, and states conditions under which catching is plausible, risky, or impossible.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true.
items.original_question: 假设你有一艘绕地球轨道运行的宇宙飞船，你能通过向另一个方向击打高尔夫球来推动你的飞船达到超过逃逸速度的速度吗？如果是这样，需要多少个高尔夫球才能到达月球？

rubrics.question_focus: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?

criteria.name: Counterfactual framing and endpoint interpretation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly interprets the premise: whether the golf balls are being sent to the Moon, or astronauts are trying to propel themselves/spacecraft by striking balls, and evaluates the appropriate endpoint under that interpretation.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the scenario or gives a joke answer with no clear endpoint.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one possible interpretation but leaves the goal or outcome vague.
criteria.5-6: States a plausible interpretation and gives a basic yes/no outcome.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes ball-reaching-Moon from astronaut-propulsion interpretations and evaluates both reasonably.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly frames all major interpretations, states which is being analyzed, and ties each to a physically consistent endpoint.

criteria.name: Momentum and delta-v fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses use of conservation of momentum, realistic golf-ball mass, swing speed, recoil, and delta-v limits for astronauts or spacecraft in orbit.
criteria.1-2: Ignores momentum or assumes hitting balls provides magical propulsion.
criteria.3-4: Mentions recoil or speed but with major physical errors.
criteria.5-6: Uses conservation of momentum qualitatively and recognizes tiny astronaut/spacecraft delta-v.
criteria.7-8: Includes approximate masses, speeds, or delta-v comparisons showing why propulsion is negligible.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively and correctly compares golf-ball impulse to lunar-transfer delta-v and cumulative ball requirements.

criteria.name: Orbital mechanics and lunar-transfer reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about launching from orbit to the Moon, including trajectory, escape/transfer velocity, targeting, timing, and relative motion.
criteria.1-2: Treats space as a straight-line shot with no orbital mechanics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions gravity or orbit but gives an incoherent trajectory.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that reaching the Moon requires correct velocity and direction, not just speed.
criteria.7-8: Explains lunar-transfer requirements, phasing, and likely miss/return/reentry outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates orbital speed, transfer injection, lunar interception, and perturbations into the causal chain.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage under real space conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of relevant mechanisms: spacesuit mobility, anchoring, club-ball contact, absence of atmosphere, spin, ball heating/reentry risk, tracking, and resource constraints.
criteria.1-2: Ignores practical mechanisms and environmental constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two space conditions superficially.
criteria.5-6: Covers several practical factors but omits important constraints.
criteria.7-8: Explains how microgravity, suit limitations, anchoring, and vacuum affect the attempt.
criteria.9-10: Provides a well-rounded mechanism analysis connecting operational constraints to trajectory and final outcome.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence and uncertainty calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent chain from swing to immediate impulse to orbital evolution to Moon encounter or failure, while calibrating uncertainty rather than overclaiming.
criteria.1-2: Uses contradictory claims or unsupported certainty.
criteria.3-4: Has a simple causal story but contains gaps or contradictions.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent sequence with some uncertainty acknowledged.
criteria.7-8: Tracks downstream effects over time and notes sensitivity to swing speed, aim, timing, and starting orbit.
criteria.9-10: Gives a contradiction-free, long-range causal analysis with explicit conditional outcomes and well-calibrated uncertainty.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force.
items.original_question: 我偶尔会在限速标志上看到“雷达强制执行”，我不禁要问：无线电波必须有多强才能阻止汽车超速，如果尝试这样做会发生什么？

rubrics.question_focus: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?

criteria.name: Radiation-pressure mechanism and force scaling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly explains how radar/radio waves could exert a stopping force on a car and scales that force with beam power.
criteria.1-2: Misses or denies electromagnetic radiation pressure, or treats radar as mechanically pushing air/car without physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions radio waves exert force but gives no usable relation between power, momentum, and force.
criteria.5-6: Uses the core scaling that force is roughly power divided by speed of light, with some simplification.
criteria.7-8: Correctly distinguishes absorption vs reflection and relates force to P/c or 2P/c for a beam on the car.
criteria.9-10: Accurately derives/uses momentum flux, notes coupling limits from imperfect reflection/absorption and beam interception area.

criteria.name: Stopping requirement and order-of-magnitude estimate
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer estimates the force/power needed to stop a plausible speeding car over a stated time or distance.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative stopping requirement or gives physically impossible magnitudes without reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague 'huge power' claim with weak or inconsistent numerical support.
criteria.5-6: Estimates car mass, speed, and deceleration, producing a roughly plausible large force.
criteria.7-8: Combines car momentum/energy with radiation pressure to obtain power around terawatts for second-to-tens-of-seconds stopping.
criteria.9-10: Clearly states assumptions and computes consistent ranges for mass, speed, stopping time/distance, force, and radar power.

criteria.name: Downstream physical effects of such radar power
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of major consequences that would occur before or alongside stopping the car.
criteria.1-2: Ignores heating, ionization, beam damage, and environmental effects entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or heat generically but not tied to the estimated radar power.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that absorbed radar energy would severely heat or damage the car/occupants.
criteria.7-8: Explains that required power would likely burn, melt, vaporize, or ionize material/air before cleanly stopping the car.
criteria.9-10: Integrates thermal absorption, plasma/air breakdown, beam spreading, shielding/reflection, and collateral hazards into the causal chain.

criteria.name: Long-range counterfactual coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent causal chain under the premise of using radar to stop a speeding car.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to unrelated technologies or conclusions with no causal link to radar stopping.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but mixes incompatible mechanisms or unexplained assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent sequence from radar beam to force to deceleration to side effects.
criteria.7-8: Handles multiple steps consistently, including source power, coupling to the car, stopping dynamics, and consequences.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust counterfactual scenario with clear assumptions, no hidden mechanism swaps, and coherent near- and downstream effects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer is appropriately cautious about assumptions while avoiding contradictions with electromagnetism and vehicle dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims, such as ordinary police radar could stop cars, or contradicts itself.
criteria.3-4: Contains major numerical or conceptual inconsistencies despite some correct ideas.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges assumptions but may overstate precision or omit key caveats.
criteria.7-8: Uses ranges and caveats for car size, speed, stopping distance, reflection, and absorption without undermining the conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, checks units/orders of magnitude, and consistently supports the conclusion that the radar would need absurdly enormous power.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per m...

rubrics.question_focus: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Boundary Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the scenario as releasing the dissolved/pressurized CO2 contained in bottled soda into the atmosphere, while defining reasonable scope assumptions about quantity, timing, and whether replacement production is included.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise, e.g., treats all soda liquid as CO2 or assumes impossible chemistry without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes soda CO2 is released but leaves scope vague or makes major unsupported assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Frames the release correctly and states some assumptions, but misses key boundaries such as global quantity or one-time vs ongoing release.
criteria.7-8: Clearly defines the release, timing, and scope, with mostly reasonable assumptions about bottled soda inventories/production.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes one-time stock from annual production, and avoids conflating soda CO2 with other carbon sources.

criteria.name: Quantitative Scale and Atmospheric Impact
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer estimates the amount of CO2 in bottled soda and compares it to atmospheric CO2 mass, ppm changes, and human annual emissions at the correct order of magnitude.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative comparison or claims catastrophic atmospheric change without scale.
criteria.3-4: Uses numbers but with severe order-of-magnitude errors or misleading comparisons.
criteria.5-6: Gives a rough scale estimate and concludes the effect is small, but calculations are incomplete or weakly justified.
criteria.7-8: Reasonably estimates soda CO2 and compares it to atmospheric CO2 or annual emissions, supporting a small-effect conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Provides transparent order-of-magnitude calculations showing the release is tiny relative to atmospheric CO2 and industrial emissions.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage Across Physical and Environmental Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of relevant mechanisms: dissolution and degassing, atmospheric mixing, greenhouse forcing, ocean/land carbon cycling, local indoor or confined-space effects, and negligible direct toxicity at global scale.
criteria.1-2: Ignores mechanisms or invents irrelevant effects such as ozone destruction or explosive global reactions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions only one mechanism, such as greenhouse warming, with little explanation.
criteria.5-6: Covers basic degassing and climate relevance but omits several important pathways or caveats.
criteria.7-8: Explains most key mechanisms, including atmospheric dilution and why global environmental effects are minimal.
criteria.9-10: Integrates all major mechanisms coherently, including local concentration risks versus negligible global climate and ecological impacts.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible downstream consequences over time, from immediate release through atmospheric mixing and climate implications, without exaggerating impacts.
criteria.1-2: Presents incoherent or fantastical chains, such as mass suffocation or immediate runaway warming.
criteria.3-4: Lists consequences without connecting them causally or temporally.
criteria.5-6: Gives a plausible short-term chain but weakly handles longer-term atmospheric and carbon-cycle outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Connects immediate, medium-term, and long-term effects in a logical sequence with proportionate impacts.
criteria.9-10: Provides a well-structured causal timeline showing rapid dilution, tiny ppm contribution, minimal warming, and eventual carbon-cycle absorption.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer clearly marks uncertainties in soda production, carbonation levels, and release assumptions while avoiding internal contradictions and unsupported certainty.
criteria.1-2: Is internally contradictory or confidently asserts false precise outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Contains multiple inconsistencies or unsupported claims, with little uncertainty acknowledgment.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but gives overprecise estimates or underexplains uncertain inputs.
criteria.7-8: Acknowledges key uncertainties and maintains consistent conclusions across the response.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, uses ranges or approximations appropriately, and keeps all assumptions and conclusions mutually consistent.

rubrics.question_focus: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup and trajectory realism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames what it means to 'throw' a tungsten countertop into the Sun, including human-scale throwing limits, Earth/Solar System orbital mechanics, and the need to cancel Earth's orbital velocity to actually fall into the Sun.

criteria.name: Tungsten material behavior under solar heating

criteria.3-4: Mentions high melting point but misstates whether solar conditions exceed it.

criteria.name: Solar-atmosphere interaction and penetration depth

criteria.name: Downstream effects on the Sun and surroundings

criteria.1-2: Predicts catastrophic solar effects or ignores consequences entirely.
criteria.3-4: States it disappears but gives no account of where the material or energy goes.
criteria.5-6: Notes that the Sun is essentially unaffected, with minimal explanation.

criteria.9-10: Covers mass/energy scale, mixing into plasma, observational insignificance, and rejects dramatic effects.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain from launch to final fate, uses appropriate scale estimates or comparisons, and avoids contradictory claims about survivability, temperature, gravity, or solar impact.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or physically impossible steps central to the answer.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct facts but an incoherent or self-contradictory causal sequence.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but lacks scale calibration or contains minor unsupported leaps.
criteria.7-8: Gives a well-ordered causal chain with reasonable qualitative or quantitative scale checks.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly consistent, uncertainty-aware explanation with clear assumptions and no significant contradictions.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?

criteria.name: Coverage of major downstream systems

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control

criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, notes that the scenario requires impossible spin-up/structural support, and keeps all downstream reasoning consistent with conservation laws and known physics.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny.
items.original_question: 如果下雨的话，挡风玻璃会被雨打碎，你需要以多快的速度行驶？

rubrics.question_focus: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and endpoint framing
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual: a vehicle or object moving through rain so fast that raindrop impacts would fracture the windshield before speed-related aerodynamic forces or other speed effects become the limiting cause.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats ordinary rain as breaking windshields at normal driving speeds.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes rain impact is relevant but gives no clear ordering against speed/aerodynamic failure.
criteria.5-6: States that extremely high speed is needed and that raindrop impact must beat other failure modes.
criteria.7-8: Clearly compares raindrop impact damage with aerodynamic pressure, heating, and structural limits.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the endpoint as an extreme-speed threshold where rain impact plausibly precedes other speed-induced windshield failure.

criteria.name: Raindrop impact physics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanism by which tiny raindrops could damage glass at extreme relative velocity, including kinetic energy, momentum, pressure, droplet size, and impact concentration.
criteria.1-2: Provides no physical mechanism or claims rain acts like a solid object without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions speed or force vaguely but ignores droplet size and impact pressure.
criteria.5-6: Explains that impact energy or pressure scales strongly with velocity and raindrops are small.
criteria.7-8: Connects droplet mass, velocity squared energy scaling, impact time/area, and windshield fracture.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent high-speed impact model, noting tiny droplets require enormous velocities to deliver damaging localized pressures.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows downstream effects over time rather than stopping at the first impact, including repeated impacts, crack initiation, crack growth, visibility loss, airflow, and vehicle survivability.
criteria.1-2: Gives an isolated conclusion with no causal sequence.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but in a disconnected or implausible order.
criteria.5-6: Describes a basic chain from impacts to chips, cracks, and failure.
criteria.7-8: Extends the chain through repeated rain impacts, crack propagation, airflow loading, and operational consequences.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a detailed, ordered chain from microscopic impacts to catastrophic windshield/vehicle failure while preserving the counterfactual ordering.

criteria.name: Competing mechanisms and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Checks whether the response avoids contradictions and accounts for competing high-speed phenomena such as air drag, bow shock, heating, compressive pressure, wiper failure, and vehicle structural failure.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself or ignores obvious speed-related effects entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some competing effects but makes inconsistent claims about which occurs first.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that drag, heating, or vehicle failure may occur before rain damage.
criteria.7-8: Explains why these competing mechanisms make the counterfactual difficult and constrain the answer.
criteria.9-10: Carefully controls contradictions by distinguishing the hypothetical rain-first condition from likely real-world limits.

criteria.name: Quantitative plausibility and uncertainty calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives appropriately cautious estimates or scaling arguments for the required speed, consistent with the fact that raindrops are tiny and the needed speed would be very high.
criteria.1-2: Gives wildly ordinary speeds or unjustified certainty.
criteria.3-4: Says only 'very fast' without scale or caveats.
criteria.5-6: Provides a rough high-speed estimate or qualitative scaling with some uncertainty.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible orders of magnitude and notes sensitivity to droplet size, glass strength, and rain intensity.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty well, using defensible scaling to show why the threshold is extreme and assumption-dependent.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses.
items.original_question: 喝醉人的血会醉吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?

criteria.name: Ethanol Dose and Blood-Volume Quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from a drunk person's blood alcohol concentration to the amount of ethanol obtained by drinking their blood, including the need for a very large volume of blood to feel alcohol effects.
criteria.1-2: Claims a small sip or glass of drunk blood would intoxicate you, with no quantitative reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes alcohol is present in the blood but badly overestimates its intoxicating dose or ignores volume.
criteria.5-6: States that a lot of blood would be needed but gives vague or partially incorrect quantities.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains that typical BAC contains little ethanol per volume and that many glasses/liters would be required.
criteria.9-10: Accurately quantifies the scale, e.g. roughly 5 liters/14 glasses of total blood in a person and only small ethanol amounts per glass, making intoxication by drinking blood implausible before other harms.

criteria.name: Digestive and Metabolic Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes drinking blood from receiving a transfusion and accurately describes digestion, absorption of ethanol, and metabolism.
criteria.1-2: Treats drinking blood as if the donor's drunkenness directly transfers into the drinker or their bloodstream.
criteria.3-4: Mentions digestion or alcohol absorption but confuses major mechanisms, such as implying intact blood enters circulation.
criteria.5-6: Explains that swallowed blood is digested and ethanol can be absorbed, but omits key limits or metabolism.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes ingestion from transfusion and describes digestion, ethanol absorption, and liver metabolism in a plausible sequence.
criteria.9-10: Provides a precise causal account: blood proteins/cells are digested, ethanol is absorbed like any alcohol, then metabolized, with dose limited by BAC and consumed volume.

criteria.name: Major Downstream Health Effects Beyond Intoxication
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of likely consequences of drinking significant amounts of human blood, including nausea, vomiting, infection risk, iron load, and ethical/practical constraints.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on getting drunk and ignores other health consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that drinking blood is unpleasant or risky but gives little mechanism or prioritization.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant effects such as nausea, vomiting, or disease risk, but misses major downstream issues.
criteria.7-8: Covers several plausible outcomes, including gastrointestinal distress, pathogen exposure, and the impracticality/danger of obtaining enough blood.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the main downstream effects in order of likelihood: taste/gagging, vomiting/diarrhea, infection exposure, iron/protein burden at high volumes, and life-threatening harm to the donor before the drinker becomes drunk.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent step-by-step counterfactual chain from obtaining drunk blood to ingestion, absorption, symptoms, and limiting factors.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or fantastical outcomes with no causal sequence.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial sequence but jumps to conclusions or leaves major causal gaps.
criteria.5-6: Gives a mostly plausible short chain but underdevelops later consequences or limiting constraints.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain from volume consumed to digestion, possible ethanol effect, illness, and practical barriers.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a detailed, non-contradictory chain showing why illness, volume limits, and donor blood volume dominate over alcohol intoxication.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids unsupported certainty, handles variation in BAC/body size/tolerance, and does not contradict itself or established physiology.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims or contradicts itself, such as saying one sip both will and will not make you drunk.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct caveats but also major unsupported or contradictory statements.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but imprecise about variation in intoxication thresholds, BAC, or blood volume.
criteria.7-8: Appropriately qualifies outcomes based on donor BAC, amount consumed, drinker size/tolerance, and contamination risk.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty carefully while preserving the main conclusion: ordinary amounts would not intoxicate you, extreme volumes are impractical and medically dangerous, and exact effects vary by BAC and individual factors.
